description: Four NASA observational scientific images: Voyager Solar System mosaic, Earth topography/bathymetry, East African Rift elevation model and Agulhas ocean color. Computed visualizations are explicitly distinguished from natural photographs.

images.title: Voyager 1's distant portrait of the Solar System
images.summary: From approximately 6.4 billion kilometers away, Voyager 1 looked back on 14 February 1990 and made a 60-frame mosaic. Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune appear as tiny lights in enlarged image insets.
images.alt: Black space with a sweeping arc of pale gray Voyager camera frames and labeled small insets of six planets, including four giant planets.
images.caption: This is the Solar System as actually seen by Voyager 1, with multiple exposures arranged in a mosaic. The enlarged inset planets and gray-frame layout are a NASA presentation, not natural scale or a single shot.
images.rights: NASA/JPL space mission product generally public domain in the US under NASA image use policy; confirm NASA/JPL credits and caption before flight use.
images.processing: NASA Voyager mosaic composed of 60 photographic frames and enlargements, not a single exposure. NASA source pixels resized to a maximum 1800-pixel side and saved as quality-87 JPEG without adding or generating structures. Original source link preserved.

images.title: Earth's mountains and seafloor from space-based data
images.summary: NASA Blue Marble: Next Generation combines a February 2004 surface image with digital elevation shading over continents and bathymetric shading beneath oceans.
images.alt: A map of Earth with land cover, snow and ice, dark blue seafloor relief, and the continents in naturalistic colors.
images.caption: A global map with topographic and seafloor relief. The underlying view combines many satellite observations and elevation datasets; it is not a single full-disk photograph.
images.credit: NASA Earth Observatory / Reto Stöckli / Robert Simmon; bathymetry and topography data providers
images.rights: NASA Earth Observatory composite based on US-government and partner bathymetry data; upstream partner reuse terms require final review.
images.processing: NASA multi-observation Blue Marble data product incorporating shaded land and ocean elevation; resampled for display. NASA source pixels resized to a maximum 1800-pixel side and saved as quality-87 JPEG without adding or generating structures. Original source link preserved.

images.title: East African Rift in the Crater Highlands
images.summary: Shuttle Radar Topography Mission data depict the Crater Highlands of northern Tanzania, where movement between the African and Somali crustal plates, volcanism and erosion shape a dramatic landscape.
images.alt: Scientific three-dimensional perspective image of cratered highlands and volcanic cones in northern Tanzania with green valleys and tan mountain slopes.
images.caption: Computer-rendered terrain from the SRTM elevation dataset, February 2000; elevation color is coded and vertical relief is exaggerated twofold. This visualization is measured data, not a natural-color aerial photograph.
images.credit: NASA / JPL / NGA Shuttle Radar Topography Mission team
images.rights: NASA/JPL/NGA scientific data rendering; official mission-source attribution provided; partner rights must be checked.
images.processing: SRTM elevation rendering with color-coded height and 2x vertical exaggeration by NASA/JPL. NASA source pixels resized to a maximum 1800-pixel side and saved as quality-87 JPEG without adding or generating structures. Original source link preserved.

images.title: Ocean currents and blooms off southern Africa
images.summary: Suomi-NPP VIIRS satellite imagery from 5 February 2018 shows swirling phytoplankton-rich water off South Africa, where warm and cold currents interact near the Cape of Good Hope.
images.alt: Wide satellite view of southern Africa with turquoise and green ribbons swirling through dark blue ocean water, and a long white cloud band offshore.
images.caption: The interaction of the Agulhas and Benguela ocean-current systems becomes visible through phytoplankton and water-color differences in this satellite composite; the image does not directly measure water speed.
images.credit: NASA Goddard Ocean Biology Processing Group / NOAA-NASA Suomi NPP VIIRS
images.rights: NASA Ocean Biology/NOAA-NASA mission observation; verify US government publication terms and instrument partner credits.
images.processing: Processed multi-band ocean-color satellite imagery, not a view of ocean current velocity. NASA source pixels resized to a maximum 1800-pixel side and saved as quality-87 JPEG without adding or generating structures. Original source link preserved.
